title: Compliance Training vs. Compliance Readiness: What 945 Leaders and Employees Told Us
summary: New Go1 research with 945 leaders and employees reveals where compliance training readiness breaks down and why scenario-based practice matters.
body_markdown:
## **Employees apply clear rules well and struggle where judgment is required**


The employee results show a clear pattern. When expectations are explicit, recently trained employees generally perform well. Among harassment-trained employees, 90% recognized that same-sex harassment is covered under federal law, one example of strong performance on a clear rule.


Accuracy drops when the correct answer depends more heavily on context. Only 39% of trained employees understood that management awareness does not eliminate a conflict of interest. Just 43% correctly distinguished a general complaint about unethical management from protected whistleblowing. Those are the kinds of boundaries that become harder to navigate when employees have to interpret a real situation rather than recall a rule.


The topic-level results tell the same story, with employees scoring 70% on harassment prevention scenarios, 56% on conflict of interest and code of conduct, and 69% on whistleblower protection.


The pattern also extends across industries. Among the larger industry groups in the sample, average scenario performance remained below 70%, with directional averages ranging from 60% in healthcare to 68% in financial and professional services. That suggests applied compliance judgment is not a challenge confined to one sector.


The weakest results consistently appeared in gray-area situations. That is where realistic scenario practice can add something a conventional knowledge check cannot: a chance to apply policy, make a decision and get feedback before the stakes are real.


It is also the thinking behind[Go1 Immersive Simulations](https://www.go1.com/immersive-simulations) , which give employees opportunities to practice applying compliance policies in realistic workplace scenarios rather than relying only on knowledge recall.


## **Why compliance training completion doesn't prove readiness**


The way organizations measure compliance training helps explain why the readiness conversation is changing. About 30% of leaders said their compliance approach primarily records completion, and roughly 38% focus on assessments. Fewer than one in five prioritize reinforcement or proactively identifying risk before incidents occur.


Completion data proves training happened, and assessments add evidence of understanding at a point in time. But the report shows that measurement changes as compliance programs mature. Outcome- and risk-oriented measures rise from 27% among completion-recording organizations to 43% among proactive-risk organizations, while audit readiness rises from 7% to 20%. The question shifts from whether training happened to what evidence shows employees are prepared to act.


## **Why stronger compliance readiness signals matter**


The stakes become clearer in the incident data. More than half of compliance and HR/L&D leaders said their organization experienced a compliance incident in the past year that additional training, reinforcement or earlier intervention may have helped prevent. That does not mean training caused those incidents, but it does show why organizations are looking for stronger signals before a problem reaches that point.


The same tension appears around risk. About 9 in 10 leaders are confident their organization can identify risk before an incident occurs, while identifying risk before incidents occur is also the most frequently cited operational challenge, at 23%. Those findings can coexist: confidence is high, but leaders are still looking for better ways to see where support is needed early enough to act.


Coverage adds another layer of complexity. Only 43% of employees had completed whistleblower protection training in the past year, compared with 81% for harassment prevention and 74% for conflict of interest or code of conduct. Whistleblower protection therefore presents two challenges in the research: fewer employees reported receiving the training, while trained employees showed uncertainty around some of the more complex boundaries of protected reporting.


## **Broad compliance training builds a baseline. Contextual practice builds on it.**


In both leader surveys, assigning compliance training to all employees is the most common approach, well ahead of assignment by role, function or risk level. Broad assignment builds a shared baseline, and there's value in everyone learning the same foundations.


The employee results add context to that assignment model. Several of the lowest-scoring questions involve situations where the right answer changes with the specifics, such as where the legal threshold for harassment sits or how far whistleblower protections extend. Broad training can establish a shared baseline, but role- and risk-relevant practice can better prepare employees for the judgment calls they are actually likely to face.


## **How scenario-based compliance training helps build applied judgment**


The encouraging part of this research is that leaders already recognize the importance of follow-through. About 8 in 10 say they always or often reinforce compliance learning after training, yet fewer than 1 in 5 describe reinforcement as the primary approach guiding their program. Reinforcement is happening in many organizations, but the report suggests it is not yet consistently treated as part of the core operating model for readiness.


Investment plans point in the same direction, with about one-third of leaders planning to invest in reinforcement after training and 27% to 28% planning to invest in scenario-based learning. When we asked leaders what would give them greater confidence in employee readiness, their open-ended answers kept returning to real-world practice, ongoing knowledge checks and accessible guidance in the moment of need.


So the questions worth asking of any compliance program are fairly simple ones.


- Does learning continue after the completion record is filed, or does the program go quiet until next year's assignment?
- Do employees get practice making the kinds of decisions their roles actually produce, in the gray areas where judgment breaks down?
- When someone misunderstands a policy, can we identify it through practice and assessment, or do we only discover it after something goes wrong?


In practice, building judgment can start small. A short scenario refresher gives someone a realistic decision to practice before the stakes arrive. Follow-up knowledge checks can show whether understanding is holding up, while managers can reinforce the gray areas their teams actually encounter. Together, those touchpoints give organizations more evidence about where employees are ready and where targeted support is still needed.


## **Moving from compliance training completion to readiness**


Compliance readiness changes what organizations count as proof. Completion remains essential, but the report’s maturity curve shows a progression from recording activity and testing understanding toward practice, reinforcement and evidence that employees can act correctly in real situations. The goal is a clearer view of readiness before risk becomes an incident.
